title: Do this for a commemoration of me (Luke 22:14–20)
word: Do this for a commemoration of m
hook: Luke's words of institution, the root of the Mass

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow's two coins and the Temple's great stones. Your line was what lasts. What did you give with your whole heart? Day four hundred seventy-nine.

Somewhere in the world, right now, a priest is holding up bread and saying words that were first spoken in an upstairs room in Jerusalem. Catholic priests celebrate Mass every day in almost every time zone, so as the earth turns, the words are nearly always being said somewhere. Today we come to that room. Jesus has sent Peter and John ahead to prepare the Passover, and they've found a large upper room, furnished, just as he said. The hour comes, and he sits down at table with the apostles. Today, the words at the root of the Mass.
screen: `A PRIEST, RIGHT NOW, SOMEWHERE.` → `A LARGE UPPER ROOM, FURNISHED.` → `THE HOUR COMES.`

segments.voice: Luke begins with longing. Jesus says: "With desire I have desired to eat this pasch with you, before I suffer." A Hebrew way of saying: I have wanted this so much. Then something only Luke records clearly: two cups. Early in the meal Jesus takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them to share it, saying he won't drink again of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom comes. The Passover meal had several cups of wine, so this fits the shape of the feast. Then the bread: "And taking bread, he gave thanks, and brake; and gave to them, saying: This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." And after supper, the second cup: "This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you." Now, today's word. Commemoration, in the Greek, is anamnesis. It doesn't mean a nostalgic memory, like looking at an old photo. In Jewish Passover practice, remembering makes the saving event present: families speak as if they themselves came out of Egypt. Catholics believe that at Mass the one sacrifice of Christ is made present, not repeated, and that the bread and wine become his body and blood, which the Church calls transubstantiation. The Council of Trent also taught that with the words do this, Christ made the apostles priests. Other Christians understand these words in different ways: many Protestants see the supper as a memorial and a meal of faith. All of them start from this same table and this same command. Notice its size. Not believe this, or understand this, first. Do this.
screen: `WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED.` · `TWO CUPS IN LUKE.` · `THIS IS MY BODY, GIVEN FOR YOU.` · `ANAMNESIS: MEMORY MADE PRESENT.` · then, large: `DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the Last Supper at table. Settle, and breathe. Think about your next meal today. Picture the table, the plate, who'll be there, or that you'll be alone. Now picture, gently, that upper room: thirteen people, bread, a cup, a man who knew what was coming and still gave thanks. When you sit down to eat today, pause for one breath before the first bite. If you pray, give thanks the way he did. If you don't, simply remember that night and the people at it. The bell holds the time.
Do this for a commemoration of me. Jesus' command over the bread in Luke, the words of institution at the root of every Mass. Today's word.
screen: `DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: do this. Today, at one meal, pause before eating and remember the upper room. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: At every Mass the priest repeats the words of institution over the bread and wine, and Catholics kneel or bow at the elevation; on Holy Thursday the Church celebrates the Mass of the Lord's Supper, remembering this night.

original.note: Greek: remembrance, commemoration. In Catholic theology, the memorial that makes Christ's sacrifice present.

trapdoor: what you thought: do this means remember Jesus fondly over a meal.
what it means: Catholics believe this command makes Christ's one sacrifice present at every Mass, with the bread and wine becoming his body and blood.
what a scholar hears: anamnesis echoes Passover memorial (zikkaron, Exodus 12:14); Trent (Session 22, canon 2) taught do this ordained the apostles priests.
